posts.author: John Sonley
posts.content_md:
Since changing the gantry and overall set-up of my sandboxed based holography table to use most of the 6' X 5' surface area, I noticed when making H2s in particular, that the reference beam drifted off the plateholder slowly over a 12 - 24 hour period. It was still stable enough to make bright H2s - but I didn't like it as H2s would be brighter without ANY movement!

This drift was noticed first of all during some very cold weather we were experiencing in N. Yorkshire - about -8 deg at night up to about +5 deg during the day. My 1st thoughts were that the slight temperature fluctuations in my basement lab was causing the air in the 6 scooter tyres upon which my sandbox sits to change volume in some non-even manner and thereby distort the table. I installed a pulse proportional heater into the airspace below my box, skirted off the temperature controlled area and confirmed a temperature stability if circa 0.1 deg ..................and the ref. beam drift was just as bad!

After two weeks of detailed study into the instability of the ref beam, undertaking selective testing of temperature effects on a range of the optical components I use, I eventually homed-in on the source of the instability which has provided the solution - and it's simple really.

 My 30 mW HeNe requires about 3 days to fully stabilise !!! - all the rest of the components - and the box are already beautifully stable over a tested temperature range in the lab of 12.8 - 16.8 deg

I've now had the ref beam centred on a white painted sheet of glass in the filmholder slot for 36 hours and the beam has not shifted one iota - QED

I had a good chat about the problem with Dave Battin on Skype a couple of days ago - I'm pleased to be able to give you some good news Dave!

I would be interested to hear from fellow members on how long you leave your HeNe 'on' to warm up before firing-off to expose a hologram

BRgds

John

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: You're talking about beam pointing stability. Is your laser mounted on its side? If so, that would increase the time to stability. He-ne lasers are generally pretty good as far as beam pointing is concerned. Are you certain it's not the mount for it that's heating up under the laser head, and bending a bit? I always use two transfer mirrors between the laser head and the first component on the table to be able to constantly adjust the position of the input beam. An iris diaphram after the spatial filters also helps in keeping the beams centered.

posts.author: Jeffrey Weil
posts.content_md:
If the beam is wandering a bit over 12 hours it won't be a problem. Any motion before the beam splitter won't matter as long as the wander doesn't cause your spatial filters to go out of focus. 

You're not losing any brightness. 

I used to let my He/Ne heat up for about an hour. Same with my He/Cd. Warming them up isn't about pointing it's about frequency stability. If the resonator is heating up, the frequency of the emitted light is going to change over time. If that's going on during an exposure your going to get "moving" fringes even without table motion. The pitch of the interference will shift with that frequency drift. 

The resonator comes to thermal equilibrium quickly. It's close to or even part of the heat source. 

The only time drifting over 12 hours would be a problem is if you had a 12 hour, or close to it, exposure and you lost either spatial filter lock or uneven exposure. 

 Jeff

> **Jeffrey Weil:** Joe, under those conditions if you make an exposure before the 4 hours are up do you lose any brightness or just pointing stability?How do you measure that, what observed condition lets you know it's at equilibrium?

Hi Jeff,

I've never noticed any pointing stability problems with the SP-127. The 4 hours refers to fringe drift. I should have mentioned that I keep the lab cool when not in use (I live in a cold climate) with the thermostat at 10C. My working temperature inside the lab is usually around 18C, so when I turn on the laser, I also raise the thermostat from 10 to 18. However, my presence in the lab (moving around, breathing, etc.) will mess up this stability. I monitor the fringes by video.

For making exposures, settling times will be important, that's why I think fringe-locking will be helpful, it really reduces settling times.

posts.author: BobH
posts.content_md: Perhaps in your focus on preventing air currents from getting at the recording system, you have cut off air flow that's necessary for proper cooling of the laser head. The set-up hates air flow. The laser head needs lots of it! It's not the plasma tube that's bending, it's the resonator. I recommend ducting outside air to flow around the head, and best if it is guided to enter the head from underneath and with fan assist. That has worked very well for me in the past, for getting the head to stay at a stable temperature after a short warm-up.

posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** John Sonley wrote:The HeNe's a 20mW Melles Griot, about 1 metre in length and it's mounted on a wooden plank on the top edge of the sand boxCould the wood be warping and/or expanding/contracting very slightly due to humidity variations? What kind of wood?

That's a very good observation and quite possibly the source of the problem. I don't have any data for expansion versus humidity variations for wood, but I would assume it's substantial. I do have some data for coefficient of thermal expansion, from "Building Scientific Apparatus" (Moore/Davis/Coplan, 2nd edition 1989), page 11:

Douglas fir (air-dried): 6 parallel to fiber (grain) and 35 across fiber

Oregon white oak (air dried) (probably similar to English oak): 5 parallel to fiber and 55 across fiber

As can be seen, the expansion parallel to the grain is remarkably good (by comparison, aluminum is 23, cast iron is 11, and invar is 1.3) but across the grain, it's not so hot. (Wood usually warps across the grain.) But this just addresses temperature, things could easily get worse when humidity fluctuations are thrown into the equation.

posts.author: John Sonley
posts.content_md:
Let me begin by thanking you all so much for your comments, so let's take them in turn: 

1. My HeNe is a Melle's Griot 05-LHP- 828 30 mW laser with a measured power output of exactly 30 mW when I last tested it

2. I haven't undertaken any interferometer tests since posting this thread as the testing I am doing is in the form of long-term tests and with such testing you only change one thing at a time. 

The 1st thing I tested was to see if temperature variations below the sand table in the vicinity of the six pneumatic tyres upon which the sand table sits was causing the variation. This airspace is now skirted off and controlled with a pulse proportional temperature controller and the temperature maintained within 0.1 degree. This action produced no improvement in the stability of my reference beam. 

The 2nd test was to vary the lab. temperature over the range it experiences in a typical year, holding it constant for several hours at each step, again no significant change was noticed and the instability of the reference beam remained as before. 

The 3rd test which I am now completing is with regard to time to see if the movement of the reference beam is reproducible and I'm pleased to report that from my test of this morning, after the laser had been switched on for 48 hours, indicates that the beam is now coming back on to the plate and I would expect by tomorrow morning it to be fully centred on the plate 

3. Bob, I am certain that the drift I'm experiencing is purely beam pointing variations as I have produced hundreds of successful holograms both H1 and H2 after the laser has been switched on for only 2 to 3 hours. This present study is for my convenience so that I don't have to readjust the spatial filter for each hologram. I want to know what warm-up time my system requires so that the reference beam will hold a quite stable beam on the film plate for a period of more than one hour, which is the settling time I give to my film temporarily laminated on to glass, prior to an exposure 

Jeffrey - I agree, on occasions a sand table is a pain - and the sand gets everywhere particularly between the glass plates scratching them and it’s even more fun when I get in the fine threads of the spatial filter adjustments screws - but I've learned to live with it

Ed, all noted about the vibrator. 2 or 3 years ago I found something else buried in the sand. My wife adores cats and our two cats discovered that my sand box was considerably more comfortable when performing their ablutions than digging a hole in the garden, this passed unnoticed for several months - at a time when I was not actively engaged in holography. Not a nice job cleaning it out. 

So in summary gentleman, I believe I now have the answer to my problem. For whatever reason, to achieve the pointing accuracy I require that allows the reference beam to remain absolutely stable on the temporary laminated H2 film-on-glass for a period of one hour, the settling time I give prior to each exposure, I think I need to switch my laser on the day before. Thank you all so much for your help and I do so wish that knowledgeable forums such as this had been available when I was going through the steepest learning curve upon starting holography about 25 years ago 

Best regards 

John
